analysis.one_liner: Banned older, noisier jets from flying to or from airports in the 20 largest metro areas.
analysis.headline: Despite 24 bipartisan cosponsors, the bill died in a House Aviation subcommittee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have made it illegal to fly any civil subsonic turbojet that does not meet 'stage 3' federal noise standards into or out of any airport in the 20 most populated U.S. metropolitan areas [S2]. Stage 2 jets are the older, louder generation of jets, and the people who live under flight paths near big-city airports bear the noise. The bill never moved beyond being referred to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and its Aviation Subcommittee [S5].
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of the neighborhoods around major airports in the largest metro areas, who would get relief from the loudest category of jet noise, including sleep disruption and other noise-related health burdens. The people who live near airports like Teterboro in the sponsor's New Jersey district are a prime example of who would benefit.

how_it_helps.text: Prohibits operating any civil subsonic turbojet that fails stage 3 noise levels to or from airports in the 20 most populated U.S. metropolitan areas [S2].
The ban applies immediately upon enactment, with no phase-in period, so noise relief would start as soon as the law took effect [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Owners and operators of older stage 2 jets — largely corporate jet owners, charter operators, and some freight operators — who would have had to retrofit engines with hushkits or retire aircraft early to keep serving big-city airports. Because the bill covered only the 20 largest metro areas, the cost would concentrate on operators serving those cities.

drawbacks.text: Compliance costs: operators of stage 2 jets would have to pay for engine hushkits or early retirement of aircraft, and small charter and freight operators would feel that cost most sharply [S2].

The bill was partly redundant: federal rules already required nearly all civil jets to meet stage 3 standards by the end of 2000, so the bill's main effect would have been to accelerate that transition in the biggest metro areas — a faster deadline, with faster costs, for a benefit that was largely coming anyway.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit — quieter neighborhoods for millions of people living near big-city airports — is broad and real, and the cost falls on a comparatively small group of older-jet operators. The main honest objection is that federal law was already phasing stage 2 jets out nationwide by the end of 2000, so this bill's added value was mostly speed in the largest metros, and it imposed that cost with no phase-in. Weighed plainly, the benefits to airport-area residents outweighed the concentrated compliance costs, though a more gradual timeline would have softened the burden on small operators.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee the day it was introduced, handed to the Aviation Subcommittee the next day, and never heard from again — no hearing, no vote, and it died when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Steven Rothman introduced the Aircraft Noise Reduction Act of 1999 on February 3, 1999 [S1].
The bill was referred to the House Committee on Transportation and Infrastructure on the day of introduction, and to the Subcommittee on Aviation the following day [S5].
No further action was ever taken; the complete action history ends with the subcommittee referral, and the bill never received a hearing or a vote [S5].
The bill attracted 24 cosponsors, 19 Democrats and 5 Republicans, showing support across both parties [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Operators of older, noisier stage 2 jets — corporate jet owners, charter companies, and freight operators — came out ahead, because they kept the right to fly those aircraft into and out of the busiest metropolitan airports without facing an early deadline to quiet or retire them. Airport-area residents, who would have gained the noise relief, got nothing.

for.name: Rep. Steven R. Rothman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to ban stage 2 jets from airports in the 20 largest metro areas

for.name: 24 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill — 19 Democrats and 5 Republicans

against.name: House Transportation and Infrastructure Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on introduction and referred it to the Aviation Subcommittee; the complete action history shows no hearing, markup, or vote ever followed [S5]

against.name: Business aviation operators
against.role: Owners and operators of older stage 2 corporate and charter jets
against.what_they_did: The general aviation community has historically resisted mandatory noise deadlines that force early retirement or retrofit of older jets, since compliance costs fall directly on them

sides.party_line_note: The bill's support was bipartisan — of its 24 cosponsors, 19 were Democrats and 5 were Republicans — and there is no record of floor votes or party-line opposition, because it never advanced that far.

industries.industry: Corporate and charter jet operators (stage 2 aircraft owners)
industries.note: The bill would have barred their older, louder jets from airports in the 20 biggest metro areas immediately on enactment, forcing hushkits or early aircraft retirement [S2]. Their interest in keeping those aircraft flying ran against the interest of residents who live under the flight paths.

Major airlines were already retiring stage 2 aircraft under the nationwide stage 3 phase-out due by the end of 2000, so the bill's extra cost to them was small and temporary, while quieter skies around their hub airports benefit their neighbors and customers.
